newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico further dismantles price controls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico further dismantles price controls.

text.p: Mexico moved to free up prices of milk on Thursday, further dismantling decades-old price controls on foodstuffs that have kept large numbers of the poverty-stricken population from starvation.
From 1998, only corn-pancake tortillas will be price controlled. The flat maize cakes are eaten more widely than bread and are the basis of the average Mexican diet.
Pastuerised milk prices will go up Dec. 30 and will likely be further hiked next year and by 1998 prices will be at the whim of market supply and demand, the Trade Ministry said.

Aside tortillas, pasteurised milk was the only other foodstuff with prices controlled by the government. In recent years, Mexico has lifted restrictions on a wide range of products from beans and rice to bread, even beer.
But the government vowed to keep massive subsidies on tortillas. Mexico paid out 6.5 billion pesos on tortilla subsidies in 1996.

"In 1997, the Federal government will maintain its subsidies for prices of tortillas to allow consumers to buy this basic foodstuff at a price below that which would be the case under a free market," the Trade Ministry said.
But President Ernesto Zedillo's government did dare to raise tortilla prices 25 percent from Dec. 30, a move which will impact inflation but is unlikely to provoke social unrest.

Tortilla prices will be raised to 1.70 peso per kilo from 1.40 peso, and even the government recognises those prices are still way below the 2.50 pesos to 3.00 pesos per kilo which it estimates the pancakes would reach if allowed to be priced according to market forces.

"The subsidies make the product cheaper by between 35 and 45 percent," the ministry said, estimating that at least 345,000 tonnes of corn per month will be under the subsidy system in 1997, or at last 4.14 million tonnes next year.

The government also announced it would continue its program of direct support to the poorest of Mexican families. Currently, the government hands out one kilo of tortillas per day to 2.4 million families, benefitting 12 million Mexicans.
For milk, the plan is to phase out controls so that all areas of the country have free-floating milk prices in 1998. Long lige, or ultrapasteurised milk is already control-free.

First, one liter presentations of pasteurised milk will be raised to 4.00 pesos from 3.60 pesos on Dec. 30 and in the fourth quarter of next year, an additional 20 centavo hike will kick in if industialists prove costs have also risen.

"The program agreed with industrialists and cattlemen sees that in 1998 the price of milk will be determined by supply and demand," the ministry said. No specific date was set for the total lifting of controls.

Part of the aim of the program is to reduce Mexico's heavy imports of milk powder. The nation imports around 17 percent of all milk needs, or around 4.5 million equivalent liters of milk, costing around $450 million.
Plans are to stop importing milk inside four years with dairymen promising to boost output and to start producing new, cut-price milk presentations for the working class.
